The Nepali media is calling it a political circus: former Nepali Congress leader and prime minister Sher Bahadur Deuba, belying his 80+ years, seems determined to remain at the helm of his party despite promising to step aside in the wake of the GenZ protests last year.

A report in the Kathmandu Post attributed to “senile spleen”, Deuba’s actions that are dividing the party. He refused to convene a special convention that would lay the ground for leadership transition and then went on to expel Gagan Thapa and BP Sharma, who had the backing of the majority of the party cadre.

The convention was later convened by Thapa with the backing of the Election Commission and the Supreme Court, but the battle continues.

“If Deuba and Thapa were locked in a debate over political or economic ideology and policy, one could grant them a modicum of respect,” went the analysis in the Kathmandu Post, “but there is no contest of ideas here. Both camps profess unyielding allegiance to democratic socialism. They share the same political outlook. This clash, therefore, is a naked, squalid struggle for patronage, candidate ticket distribution, and personal control over the party apparatus.”

The article faults Deuba for lacking ideas and vision at a time when a new generation of cadres are mobilising at the grassroots and filling ward positions.

“Deuba must abandon his parallel shadow-party, relinquish his suffocating grip, and urge his loyalists to enter the legitimate party under Gagan Thapa’s banner. History will cherish a leader who knows when to step off the stage. It will show no mercy to one who burns down the theatre on his way out.”

Similar theatre is being played out across the political aisle in the CPN-UML headed by former prime minister KP Sharma Oli. Recall he was the man forced to resign during the GenZ protests but somehow was able to regain control of the party apparatus.

He’s struggling to contain the ambitions of party colleague Bidya Devi Bhandari, who has been formally reinstated in the party. Note that Bhandari is a former president of Nepal, she quit her party to get that job and now, well into her sixties, she has re-entered with some calculations of her own.

In India former presidents ensure the dignity and neutrality of the office they held by staying away from politics. In Nepal however, Bhandari clearly sees no problem. Her political ambitions are evident, she has said she wants to lead the party and at some point one can expect a struggle for power with Oli.

As the Kathmandu Post notes, “Bhandari’s return may be legally permissible, but it sets a wrong precedent. It will only leave a deep scar on her already blotched record in the history books.”

title: The gap nobody is talking about: Why Nepal's stagnant child mortality rate is a warning sign - The Himalayan Times
description: The gap nobody is talking about: Why Nepal's stagnant child mortality rate is a warning sign  The Himalayan Times
publisher.title: The Himalayan Times
full_article:
Every year in Nepal, a family celebrates a pregnancy with hope, follows the antenatal visits they are told to attend, and delivers their baby in a health facility - doing everything right, by the book. And yet, for a significant number of these families, that child will grow up with a disability that could have been prevented. Not because anyone failed them individually, but because Nepal's health system has a structural blind spot that almost no one is talking about.

I have spent the past 20 years working in maternal and child health, disability prevention, and community-based rehabilitation at Karuna Foundation Nepal. In that time, I have watched Nepal make genuine, measurable progress. Institutional deliveries have risen from just 8 percent in 1996 to 79 percent today. Immunisation programmes reach the vast majority of our children. These are real achievements, and they deserve recognition.

Related Articles Building from the ground up: Why Nepal needs indigenous bridge engineering literature What the Rasuwa glacial flood reveals about Himalayan climate risks

But progress at the two ends of the journey - pregnancy care once conception has already happened, and child health once the baby has already arrived - has left a critical middle section almost entirely unaddressed. There is no organised, national programme to prepare couples for a safer pregnancy before conception. There is no systemic screening programme for the major categories of birth defects: structural and neural tube defects, hearing and vision impairments, congenital heart disease, and neurodevelopmental conditions.

And there is no routine pathway for foetal screening of conditions like Down syndrome, which families elsewhere in the world are able to know about, and prepare for, well before birth.

The consequences of this gap are not abstract. One-third of neonatal deaths in Nepal are attributed to congenital anomalies - one of the least addressed causes in our national newborn health response.

Despite folic acid's proven ability to reduce neural tube defects by up to 70 percent, only 21 percent of pregnant women in Nepal take it adequately. Only one in four of our birthing centres is properly equipped for emergency obstetric and newborn care. And our neonatal mortality rate has been stuck at 21 per 1,000 live births for years, even as institutional delivery coverage has climbed.

This stagnation is not a mystery - it is what public health experts recognise elsewhere as an epidemiological transition, and Nepal is living through its own version of it.

We have done the harder, more visible work of getting mothers to a skilled attendant and a facility bed. What remains stuck is a different category of problem entirely: congenital and non-communicable conditions present at or before birth, which do not respond to more access alone.

Expanding institutional delivery got us this far. It cannot, on its own, take us further. The children we are still losing, and the disabilities we are still failing to catch early, are being driven not by a lack of facilities, but by a lack of planning, screening, and early detection - a fundamentally different kind of intervention than the one that got Nepal from 8 percent institutional delivery to 79.

One consequence I have seen repeatedly in my own career deserves particular attention: a substantial share of children living with cerebral palsy in Nepal acquired it not from any prenatal condition, but from prolonged or poorly managed delivery - something that, with the right emergency obstetric capacity in place, is often preventable.

There is also a challenge on the horizon that Nepal is not yet prepared for. Autism and other neurodevelopmental conditions are being diagnosed at rising rates worldwide, and there is every reason to expect Nepal will see the same trend, whether or not our health system is ready to recognise it.

Early identification - ideally by age three - makes an enormous difference to a child's long-term development. Right now, Nepal has no structured system to make that early identification happen.

Nepal got mothers to health facilities. Nepal got children immunised. Those were the right first battles, and they were won. The next one is harder, because it cannot be solved by access alone - it requires catching what can be caught, preventing what can be prevented, and giving every child, not just the fortunate ones, the healthiest possible start in life.

That is not only a health question. It is one of the most cost-effective investments Nepal could make in its own future - because a disability prevented is a lifetime of care, dignity, and opportunity given back to a child and their family, at a fraction of the cost of managing that disability for decades to come.

Nepal has already shown, twice now, that it knows how to close a health gap when it decides to. The question is whether we recognise this one before another generation of children pays the cost of our not looking.

Sapkota is executive director of Karuna Foundation Nepal

KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 2 — Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah has assured Malaysia of full cooperation to determine the status of 54 citizens still missing after devastating floods and landslides in Nepal, Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim said today.

The update came after one of 55 Malaysians previously listed as missing was located safe and made contact with the Malaysian Embassy in Kathmandu, according to family representatives and official updates.

"I have had conversations with the prime minister. He is willing to give all the cooperation," Anwar said to reporters this afternoon, adding that Shah agreed during a bilateral call to facilitate administrative and legal efforts to help relatives obtain closure as quickly as possible.

The standard legal procedures in Nepal typically require a three-year waiting period to issue a death certificate for missing persons, compared to six or seven years under Malaysian law, Anwar said.

However, Nepalese authorities have agreed to support expedited court applications.

"He assured me that he will give all the cooperation necessary to facilitate so that the families can get the results as soon as possible," Anwar added.

Dr Manivannan Rethinam, a spokesman for Malaysia Solidarity: Families in Hope (MASFIH), a group representing the victims' relatives, confirmed that the Foreign Ministry had officially notified them of the located citizen, who has since returned to Malaysia.

title: Nepal plans to drain four glacial lakes after deadly floods - Internazionale
description: Nepal plans to drain four glacial lakes after deadly floods  Internazionale
publisher.title: Internazionale
full_article:
By Gopal Sharma

KATHMANDU, Oct 2 (Reuters) - Nepal will kick off a high-stakes effort this fiscal year to drain four glacial lakes perched high in the mountains, as it scrambles to reduce flood risks, officials said, after a recent disaster that killed more than 1,400.

Rescuers are still searching for more than 5,000 people missing in the border region with China after August’s glacier collapse unleashed landslides and a flash flood that tore through valleys.

“Our aim is to lower the risk of the lakes breaching their natural dams and reduce the risk of downstream floods,” said Subash Tuladhar, an expert with a government research centre tasked with overseeing the new project.

Canals will drain water into nearby rivers in a regulated way, he said, adding that workers faced health risks as a result of the lengthy periods of high-altitude work required, in addition to the dangers of sudden flooding.

Design work and detailed studies targeting the central and eastern lakes of Thulagi, Lower Barun, Lumding Tsho and Hongu II, will begin in the fiscal year that runs until mid-July 2027, authorities said.

The lakes, at heights ranging from 4,050 m to 5,483 m (13,280 ft to 18,000 ft), rank among Nepal’s most potentially dangerous, the United Nations Development Programme and the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) said in a 2020 report.

Nepal had the skills and experience required for the $50-million project to be funded by the Green Climate Fund, the UNDP and the government, added Tuladhar, of Nepal’s Centre for Hydrology and Water Resources Research.

DRAINING PROJECT COULD TAKE SIX YEARS

The work of draining “through gated structures” will start after a detailed study, and could take up to six years to complete, said Sanjeeb Baral, the Centre’s executive director.

It will encompass installation of sensors, a flood forecasting and warning system, and efforts to build downstream resilience and prepare communities for the risks.

In similar previous efforts, Nepal lowered by 3 m (10 ft) the level of the central Himalayan glacial lake of Tsho Rolpa by in 2000 and that of Imja in the vicinity of Mount Everest, the world’s tallest peak, 10 years ago.

URGENCY AFTER RECENT FLOODS

Nepal’s disaster served as a warning to the world, Prime Minister Balendra Shah, 36, told the United Nations in an impassioned speech last month that blamed climate change despite his country’s negligible emissions.

Retreating glaciers, unstable mountain slopes and increasingly unpredictable rivers showed Nepal was paying a heavy price, he added.

Nepal, which has reported about 26 Glacial Lake Outburst Flood events in the past four decades, loses more than 300 lives and property worth millions of dollars to extreme climate events annually on average.

The latest floods devastated a dozen hydroelectric plants, roads, bridges, farms and settlements. Cash-strapped Nepal would need nearly $5 billion for early recovery, officials have said.

Climate scientists say as temperatures rise glaciers in the Himalayas retreat, leaving behind ​unstable glacial lakes held back by little more than loose rock and ​ice, above valleys home to millions.

Lowering the lakes by 3 m (10 ft) would significantly reduce the threat, said Samjwal Ratna Bajracharya, a retired ICIMOD expert on glaciers, glacial lakes and outburst floods.

“They are growing fast, are high up in the Himalayas and could cause outbursts any time, due to earthquakes, avalanches, climatic conditions and unplanned human-induced activity,” he told Reuters.

(Reporting by Gopal Sharma; Editing by Aftab Ahmed and Clarence Fernandez)

title: Nepal avalanche death toll rises to 15 as 8 bodies found on Mount Himlung - tbsnews.net
description: Nepal avalanche death toll rises to 15 as 8 bodies found on Mount Himlung  tbsnews.net
publisher.title: tbsnews.net
full_article:
Rescuers recovered eight bodies from the base camp of Mount Himlung in Nepal on Thursday (1 October), raising the death toll from an avalanche during severe weather Sunday to 15.

The Nepal National Mountain Guide Association, which is leading the search operation, said rescuers dug through thick snow at the mountain's base camp and found eight bodies inside tents. One person remains missing.

"Due to continuing mountain hazards, recovery efforts have been temporarily concluded," the association said, adding that the search could resume when weather and mountain conditions improve.

full_article:
In Nepal, forensic laboratories are conducting DNA testing on thousands of samples to establish the identities of people killed in massive flooding. As Dawn reports, the country's authorities have recovered 1,454 bodies, although about one-third of them are only fragments of remains. Families have been handed over 112 identified bodies.

In Nepal, 5,285 people are missing, including hundreds of foreigners. In China, according to state media, 43 people have died and another 519 are considered missing. Overall, the death toll in the two countries is approaching 1,500, while the number of missing people is nearing 5,800.

Thousands of samples for comparison

The flooding was caused by a wave of icy water and debris that formed after a glacier and rocks collapsed on the Nepal-China border on August 26. Some bodies were carried far downstream by the water, complicating their identification.

Two forensic laboratories in Kathmandu are processing 3,685 samples, including more than 1,300 taken from recovered remains. Mukul Pradhan, chief scientific officer at the National Forensic Science Laboratory, noted that the laboratory usually analyses between 1,000 and 1,500 samples per year, mainly in paternity cases or criminal investigations.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Blood samples are easier to analyse, while examining teeth or bones can take several days. Nepalese authorities have buried more than 1,200 bodies after numbering and marking them so that the remains can be exhumed if a DNA match is established.

Help from international specialists

Nirajan Thapa, head of the biology department at the National Forensic Science Laboratory, explained that one DNA profile from remains is not enough: it must be compared with a sample from a relative. Therefore, specialists must process materials from both unidentified remains and thousands of family members of missing people.

Teams from India, China and South Korea have provided assistance to Nepal. Fingerprint experts from the United States and Singapore have also joined the work. According to Thapa's assessment, with such support, sample matching could begin within a few weeks.

Fifty-three-year-old Rajesh Ram, whose son Suroj Kumar went missing in flooded Betravati, told AFP that he had unsuccessfully searched for his son's body. Some families have already held symbolic cremation ceremonies for those missing.
